The type and cardinality of minimal presentations of
numerical semigroups with embedding dimension four

Kazimierz Chomicz
September 2026
Abstract

For a numerical semigroup SS with embedding dimension four, we study the relationship between its type t⁡(S)t(S) and the cardinality of its minimal presentations η⁡(S)\eta(S). Using an approach based on the geometry of the Apéry set, we prove that 4​t​(S)+5≥η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)−114t(S)+5\geq\eta(S)\geq t(S)-11. This resolves a problem of Moscariello and Sammartano asking whether t⁡(S)t(S) is bounded by a function of η⁡(S)\eta(S), and improves the previously known bound 9​t​(S)+4≥η⁡(S)9t(S)+4\geq\eta(S) due to Bresinsky.

1 Introduction

†† Keywords: numerical semigroup, embedding dimension, Apéry set, type, minimal presentation.†† 2020 Mathematics Subject Classification: 20M13, 20M14

Let ℕ\mathbb{N} denote the set of nonnegative integers. For k>0k>0 and d0,d1,…,dk∈ℕd_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\in\mathbb{N} such that gcd⁡(d0,d1,…,dk)=1\gcd(d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k})=1, the set

S=⟨d0,d1,…,dk⟩={λ0​d0+λ1​d1+⋯+λk​dk∣λi∈ℕ},S=\langle d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\rangle=\{\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\dots+\lambda_{k}d_{k}\mid\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{N}\},

is called a numerical semigroup generated by {d0,d1,…,dk}\{d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\}. Equivalently, SS is a submonoid of (ℕ,+)(\mathbb{N},+) such that ℕ∖S\mathbb{N}\setminus S is finite (see [14, Lemma 2.1]). If no proper subset of {d0,d1,…,dk}\{d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\} generates SS, then we say that SS is minimally generated by {d0,d1,…,dk}\{d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\}. The cardinality of the minimal set of generators of SS is called the embedding dimension of SS and is denoted e⁡(S)e(S).

The largest integer that is not in SS is called the Frobenius number and is denoted F⁡(S)F(S). An integer a∉Sa\notin S is called a pseudo-Frobenius number of SS if a+s∈Sa+s\in S for all s∈S∖{0}s\in S\setminus\{0\}. The set of all pseudo-Frobenius numbers of SS is denoted P​F​(S)PF(S). The cardinality of P​F​(S)PF(S) is called the type of SS and is denoted t⁡(S)t(S).

If SS is minimally generated by {d0,d1,…,dk}\{d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\}, then we have a homomorphism φ:ℕk+1→S\varphi:\mathbb{N}^{k+1}\to S defined by φ⁡(z0,…,zk)=z0​d0+⋯+zk​dk\varphi(z_{0},\dots,z_{k})=z_{0}d_{0}+\dots+z_{k}d_{k}. The kernel congruence of φ\varphi is ker⁡(φ)={(a,b)∈ℕk+1×ℕk+1∣φ⁡(a)=φ⁡(b)}\ker(\varphi)=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{k+1}\times\mathbb{N}^{k+1}\mid\varphi(a)=\varphi(b)\}. It is well known that SS is isomorphic to the monoid ℕk+1/ker⁡(φ)\mathbb{N}^{k+1}/\ker(\varphi). A minimal set of generators of the congruence ker⁡(φ)\ker(\varphi) is called a minimal presentation of SS. Minimal presentations of SS are not unique, but their cardinality depends only on SS and is denoted by η⁡(S)\eta(S).

Both type and minimal presentations are central to the study of numerical semigroups (see [2, 3, 9, 13, 14]). In the study of minimal presentations, the invariant η⁡(S)\eta(S) has attracted considerable interest (see [8, 12, 13, 14, 16]).

A numerical semigroup SS is symmetric if for every x∈ℤ∖Sx\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus S we have F⁡(S)−x∈SF(S)-x\in S. This is equivalent to t⁡(S)=1t(S)=1 [11]. It is well known that if e⁡(S)=2e(S)=2, then t⁡(S)=η⁡(S)=1t(S)=\eta(S)=1. The case e⁡(S)=3e(S)=3 is completely settled in the following theorem.

Theorem 1.1.

[10] Let SS be a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)=3e(S)=3. If SS is symmetric, then η⁡(S)=2\eta(S)=2 and t⁡(S)=1t(S)=1. If SS is not symmetric, then η⁡(S)=3\eta(S)=3 and t⁡(S)=2t(S)=2.

When e⁡(S)≥4e(S)\geq 4, the situation becomes much more complicated. Bresinsky [4] found a family of numerical semigroups with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4 whose η⁡(S)\eta(S) can be arbitrarily large, while Backelin [9, p. 75] found a family of numerical semigroups with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4 whose t⁡(S)t(S) can be arbitrarily large.

In this paper, we study t⁡(S)t(S) and η⁡(S)\eta(S) for numerical semigroups with embedding dimension four. In [6], Bresinsky established the following bound.

Theorem 1.2.

[6, Theorem 7] If SS is a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, then 9​t​(S)+4≥η⁡(S)9t(S)+4\geq\eta(S).

In [13], the authors, inspired by the above bound, proposed the following problem.

Problem 1.3.

[13, Problem 25] Let SS be a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4. Is t⁡(S)t(S) bounded by a function of η⁡(S)\eta(S)?

Resolving Problem 1.3 also settles a general problem on the boundedness of Betti numbers [13, Problem 24] in the case e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, as noted in the same paper.

The main result of this paper is the following theorem, which settles Problem 1.3 and improves the bound of Theorem 1.2.

Theorem 1.4.

If SS is a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, then 4​t​(S)+5≥η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)−114t(S)+5\geq\eta(S)\geq t(S)-11.

The paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we study the geometry of the Apéry set of numerical semigroups with embedding dimension four using LL-shapes [1]. In Section 3, we relate minimal presentations of numerical semigroups with embedding dimension four to an LL-shape. In Section 4, we prove Theorem 1.4 by using results of the previous sections to study t⁡(S)t(S) and η⁡(S)\eta(S) geometrically. We conclude the paper with Conjecture 5.1.

2 Geometry of the Apéry set

In this section, we study the geometry of the Apéry set of numerical semigroups with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4. Subsection 2.1 introduces the notion of minimal relations and uses them to classify numerical semigroups with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4 into primary and secondary semigroups (Lemma 2.2) — a distinction that underpins our approach. Subsection 2.2 presents the geometric framework for analyzing the Apéry set (Theorem 2.4). Subsection 2.3 introduces the notion of LL-shapes and examines them for primary and secondary semigroups (Propositions 2.7 and 2.8).

Let SS be minimally generated by {d0,d1,…,dk}\{d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\}. For an element s∈Ss\in S, the set

φ−1​(s)={(z0,…,zk)∈ℕk+1∣z0​d0+⋯+zk​dk=s}\varphi^{-1}(s)=\{(z_{0},\dots,z_{k})\in\mathbb{N}^{k+1}\mid z_{0}d_{0}+\dots+z_{k}d_{k}=s\} (1)

is called the set of factorizations of ss. For z=(z0,…,zk)∈φ−1​(s)z=(z_{0},\dots,z_{k})\in\varphi^{-1}(s), the support of zz is

supp​(z)={i∈{0,…,k}∣zi>0}.\text{supp}(z)=\{i\in\{0,\dots,k\}\mid z_{i}>0\}. (2)

For an element a∈Sa\in S, the set

Ap​(S,a)={s∈S∣s−a∉S}\textup{Ap}(S,a)=\{s\in S\mid s-a\notin S\} (3)

is called the Apéry set of SS with respect to aa. Note that Ap​(S,a)\textup{Ap}(S,a) is the set of the smallest nonnegative integers from each residue class modulo aa that are in SS, hence |Ap​(S,a)|=a|\textup{Ap}(S,a)|=a. From [14, Proposition 2.20], we have

PF(S)={s−a∣s∈Ap(S,a),s+di∉Ap(S,a) for i=0,1,…,k}.PF(S)=\{s-a\mid s\in\textup{Ap}(S,a),s+d_{i}\notin\textup{Ap}(S,a)\text{ for }i=0,1,\dots,k\}. (4)

This description of pseudo-Frobenius numbers in terms of the Apéry set will provide a useful framework for our study of the type in Section 4.

2.1 Minimal relations

Let S=⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩S=\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle be a numerical semigroup with embedding dimension four.

For every i∈{0,1,2,3}i\in\{0,1,2,3\}, let ai​ia_{ii} be the smallest positive integer such that there exist nonnegative integers ai​j,ai​k,ai​la_{ij},a_{ik},a_{il} satisfying

ai​i​di=ai​j​dj+ai​k​dk+ai​l​dla_{ii}d_{i}=a_{ij}d_{j}+a_{ik}d_{k}+a_{il}d_{l} (5)

where {i,j,k,l}={0,1,2,3}\{i,j,k,l\}=\{0,1,2,3\}. We call (5) a minimal relation of did_{i}.

Fix m∈{0,1,2,3}m\in\{0,1,2,3\}. For every i∈{0,1,2,3}∖{m}i\in\{0,1,2,3\}\setminus\{m\}, let bm,i​ib_{m,ii} be the smallest positive integer such that there exist nonnegative integers bm,i​j,bm,i​k,bm,i​lb_{m,ij},b_{m,ik},b_{m,il} satisfying

bm,i​i​di=bm,i​j​dj+bm,i​k​dk+bm,i​l​dlb_{m,ii}d_{i}=b_{m,ij}d_{j}+b_{m,ik}d_{k}+b_{m,il}d_{l} (6)

where {i,j,k,l}={0,1,2,3}\{i,j,k,l\}=\{0,1,2,3\} and bm,i​m>0b_{m,im}>0. We call (6) a dmd_{m}-positive minimal relation of did_{i}.

Note that in the minimal relations ai​ia_{ii} is unique; however, each ai​ja_{ij} for i≠ji\neq j is not necessarily unique. Similarly, in the dmd_{m}-positive minimal relations bm,i​ib_{m,ii} is unique; however, each bm,i​jb_{m,ij} for i≠ji\neq j is not necessarily unique.

Let φ:ℕ4→S\varphi:\mathbb{N}^{4}\to S be the factorization morphism of SS.

Lemma 2.1.

For i∈{0,1,2,3}i\in\{0,1,2,3\} and (μ0,μ1,μ2,μ3)∈φ−1​(ai​i​di)(\mu_{0},\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{ii}d_{i}), we have either μi=ai​i\mu_{i}=a_{ii} and μj=0\mu_{j}=0 for all j∈{0,1,2,3}∖{i}j\in\{0,1,2,3\}\setminus\{i\}, or μi=0\mu_{i}=0.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, suppose i=0i=0. We have

(a00−μ0)​d0=μ1​d1+μ2​d2+μ3​d3.(a_{00}-\mu_{0})d_{0}=\mu_{1}d_{1}+\mu_{2}d_{2}+\mu_{3}d_{3}. (7)

The right-hand side is clearly nonnegative. If (a00−μ0)=0(a_{00}-\mu_{0})=0, then μ1=μ2=μ3=0\mu_{1}=\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}=0. If (a00−μ0)>0(a_{00}-\mu_{0})>0, then the minimality of a00a_{00} implies μ0=0\mu_{0}=0. ∎

Proof.

Suppose that for every m∈{0,1,2,3}m\in\{0,1,2,3\} we have ai​i<bm,i​ia_{ii}<b_{m,ii} for at least two distinct indices i∈{0,1,2,3}∖{m}i\in\{0,1,2,3\}\setminus\{m\} (note that ai​i≤bm,i​ia_{ii}\leq b_{m,ii} always holds by definition).

a00​d0=a01​d1=(a01−a11)​d1+a1​i​dia_{00}d_{0}=a_{01}d_{1}=(a_{01}-a_{11})d_{1}+a_{1i}d_{i} (8)

for some i∈{0,2,3}i\in\{0,2,3\}. Clearly a1​i>0a_{1i}>0. If i=0i=0, subtracting d0d_{0} from both sides of (8) contradicts the minimality of a00a_{00}. If i≠0i\neq 0, we get a factorization z∈φ−1​(a00​d0)z\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) with |supp​(z)|=2|\textup{supp}(z)|=2, which is a contradiction.

If there exists m∈{0,1,2,3}m\in\{0,1,2,3\} such that ai​i=bm,i​ia_{ii}=b_{m,ii} for at least two distinct indices i∈{0,1,2,3}∖{m}i\in\{0,1,2,3\}\setminus\{m\}, we call ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle primary. Moreover, for a primary semigroup ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle, unless stated otherwise, we always assume throughout this paper that the generators are ordered so that a11=b0,11a_{11}=b_{0,11} and a22=b0,22a_{22}=b_{0,22}.

Numerical semigroups with embedding dimension four that are not primary will be referred to as secondary semigroups. By Lemma 2.2, if ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle is a secondary semigroup, then there exists an arrangement {i,j,k,l}={0,1,2,3}\{i,j,k,l\}=\{0,1,2,3\} such that ai​i​di=aj​j​dj≠ak​k​dk=al​l​dla_{ii}d_{i}=a_{jj}d_{j}\neq a_{kk}d_{k}=a_{ll}d_{l}, and φ−1​(ai​i​di)∪φ−1​(ak​k​dk)={(a00,0,0,0),(0,a11,0,0),(0,0,a22,0),(0,0,0,a33)}\varphi^{-1}(a_{ii}d_{i})\cup\varphi^{-1}(a_{kk}d_{k})=\{(a_{00},0,0,0),(0,a_{11},0,0),(0,0,a_{22},0),(0,0,0,a_{33})\}. Moreover, for a secondary semigroup ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle, unless stated otherwise, we always assume throughout this paper that the generators are ordered so that φ−1​(a00​d0)=φ−1​(a11​d1)={(a00,0,0,0),(0,a11,0,0)}\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0})=\varphi^{-1}(a_{11}d_{1})=\{(a_{00},0,0,0),(0,a_{11},0,0)\} and φ−1​(a22​d2)=φ−1​(a33​d3)={(0,0,a22,0),(0,0,0,a33)}\varphi^{-1}(a_{22}d_{2})=\varphi^{-1}(a_{33}d_{3})=\{(0,0,a_{22},0),(0,0,0,a_{33})\}.

A numerical semigroup with embedding dimension four, S=⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩S=\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle, is said to be ordered if its generators are arranged according to the ordering defined above — that is, the ordering assumed for primary semigroups if SS is primary, and the ordering assumed for secondary semigroups if SS is secondary. We adopt this convention so that certain definitions and constructions can be stated uniformly for any ordered semigroup ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle, without requiring a prior assumption on whether it is primary or secondary.

2.2 Geometric framework

From this point on, we will focus on the Apéry set of ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle with respect to d0d_{0}, which we henceforth refer to simply as the Apéry set. For brevity, we also write b0,i​j=bi​jb_{0,ij}=b_{ij} for all i,j∈{0,1,2,3}i,j\in\{0,1,2,3\}.

Consider the unit cubes in ℝ3\mathbb{R}^{3}. Each unit cube [i,i+1]×[j,j+1]×[k,k+1]⊂ℝ3[i,i+1]\times[j,j+1]\times[k,k+1]\subset\mathbb{R}^{3} has natural coordinates (i,j,k)∈ℕ3(i,j,k)\in\mathbb{N}^{3} and is labeled with the value i​d1+j​d2+k​d3id_{1}+jd_{2}+kd_{3}. We will refer to the collection of all such labeled cubes as the initial collection of cubes. We denote the unit cube [i,i+1]×[j,j+1]×[k,k+1][i,i+1]\times[j,j+1]\times[k,k+1] by [[i,j,k]][[i,j,k]]. For a point P=(a,b,c)∈ℤ3P=(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{Z}^{3}, we call the region {x>a,y>b,z>c}\{x>a,y>b,z>c\} the region associated to PP. We write [[a,b,c]]≥[[a′,b′,c′]][[a,b,c]]\geq[[a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}]] when a≥a′a\geq a^{\prime}, b≥b′b\geq b^{\prime}, c≥c′c\geq c^{\prime}, and [[a,b,c]]>[[a′,b′,c′]][[a,b,c]]>[[a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}]] when [[a,b,c]]≥[[a′,b′,c′]][[a,b,c]]\geq[[a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}]] and [[a,b,c]]≠[[a′,b′,c′]][[a,b,c]]\neq[[a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}]].

Lemma 2.3.

No cube labeled with an element of the Apéry set is in the region associated to a point (μ1,μ2,μ3)∈ℤ3(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})\in\mathbb{Z}^{3} satisfying μ1​d1+μ2​d2+μ3​d3=μ​d0\mu_{1}d_{1}+\mu_{2}d_{2}+\mu_{3}d_{3}=\mu d_{0} for some positive integer μ\mu.

Proof.

Recall that the Apéry set with respect to d0d_{0} is the set of the smallest nonnegative integers from each residue class modulo d0d_{0} that are in the numerical semigroup ⟨d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle. Suppose to the contrary, that for some residue r∈{0,1,…,d0−1}r\in\{0,1,\dots,d_{0}-1\} there is a cube [[λ1,λ2,λ3]][[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]] labeled with the smallest number λ​d0+r\lambda d_{0}+r (λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N}) that is in ⟨d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle such that [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]≥[[μ1,μ2,μ3]][[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\geq[[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]]. This gives

(λ1−μ1)​d1+(λ2−μ2)​d2+(λ3−μ3)​d3=(λ−μ)​d0+r(\lambda_{1}-\mu_{1})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}-\mu_{2})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}-\mu_{3})d_{3}=(\lambda-\mu)d_{0}+r (9)

where all coefficients on the left-hand side are nonnegative. This means that the value in (9) is congruent to rr modulo d0d_{0}, is nonnegative, is in ⟨d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle, and is strictly less than λ​d0+r\lambda d_{0}+r, which contradicts the minimality of λ​d0+r\lambda d_{0}+r. ∎

Theorem 2.4.

Delete from the initial collection of cubes the regions {x>b11}\{x>b_{11}\}, {y>b22}\{y>b_{22}\}, and {z>b33}\{z>b_{33}\}. Next, for every point (a01,a02,a03)∈ℕ3(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\mathbb{N}^{3} satisfying

a01​d1+a02​d2+a03​d3=a00​d0a_{01}d_{1}+a_{02}d_{2}+a_{03}d_{3}=a_{00}d_{0} (10)

delete the region associated to it. Furthermore, for all identities of the form

λ0​d0+λ1​d1=λ2​d2+λ3​d3\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{1}d_{1}=\lambda_{2}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}d_{3} (11)

with λi∈ℤ>0\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, λ2<b22\lambda_{2}<b_{22}, and λ3<b33\lambda_{3}<b_{33}, delete the region associated to (−λ1,λ2,λ3)(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}). For all identities of the form

λ0​d0+λ2​d2=λ1​d1+λ3​d3\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}=\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{3}d_{3} (12)

with λi∈ℤ>0\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, λ1<b11\lambda_{1}<b_{11}, and λ3<b33\lambda_{3}<b_{33}, delete the region associated to (λ1,−λ2,λ3)(\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}). Finally, for all identities of the form

λ0​d0+λ3​d3=λ1​d1+λ2​d2\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{3}d_{3}=\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2} (13)

with λi∈ℤ>0\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, λ1<b11\lambda_{1}<b_{11}, and λ2<b22\lambda_{2}<b_{22}, delete the region associated to (λ1,λ2,−λ3)(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3}). Then, the remaining collection of cubes is the set of all cubes from the initial collection of cubes that are labeled with an element of the Apéry set.

Proof.

Let RR be the remaining collection of cubes. The condition λi<bi​i\lambda_{i}<b_{ii} ensures that only the relevant identities are considered, since we delete the regions {x>b11}\{x>b_{11}\}, {y>b22}\{y>b_{22}\}, and {z>b33}\{z>b_{33}\}. Moreover, by Lemma 2.3, every cube labeled with an element of the Apéry set is in RR, since deleting the regions {x>b11}\{x>b_{11}\}, {y>b22}\{y>b_{22}\}, and {z>b33}\{z>b_{33}\} is the same as deleting the regions associated to (b11,−b12,−b13)(b_{11},-b_{12},-b_{13}), (−b21,b22,−b23)(-b_{21},b_{22},-b_{23}), and (−b31,−b32,b33)(-b_{31},-b_{32},b_{33}).

Therefore we only need to prove that RR contains only cubes labeled with an element of the Apéry set. Suppose to the contrary, that for some remainder r∈{0,1,…,d0−1}r\in\{0,1,\dots,d_{0}-1\}, λ​d0+r\lambda d_{0}+r and λ′​d0+r\lambda^{\prime}d_{0}+r, where λ′>λ\lambda^{\prime}>\lambda, are labels in RR. This means that

λ​d0+r=λ1​d1+λ2​d2+λ3​d3\lambda d_{0}+r=\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}d_{3} (14)
λ′​d0+r=λ1′​d1+λ2′​d2+λ3′​d3\lambda^{\prime}d_{0}+r=\lambda_{1}^{\prime}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}^{\prime}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}^{\prime}d_{3} (15)

where [[λ1,λ2,λ3]],[[λ1′,λ2′,λ3′]]∈R[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]],[[\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}]]\in R. Subtracting (14) from (15) we get

(λ′−λ)​d0=(λ1′−λ1)​d1+(λ2′−λ2)​d2+(λ3′−λ3)​d3(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda)d_{0}=(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3})d_{3} (16)

where (λ′−λ)>0(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda)>0. Now, we consider cases of how many coefficients on the right-hand side of (16) are positive. The left-hand side is positive; hence, at least one of the coefficients on the right-hand side is positive.

If exactly one coefficient is positive, without loss of generality, suppose that (λ1′−λ1)(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1}) is the one. Moving the non-positive integers to the other side gives

(λ′−λ)​d0+(λ2−λ2′)​d2+(λ3−λ3′)​d3=(λ1′−λ1)​d1.(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda)d_{0}+(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}-\lambda_{3}^{\prime})d_{3}=(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}. (17)

Since all the above coefficients are nonnegative and (λ1′−λ1)(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1}) and (λ′−λ)(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda) are positive, the minimality of b11b_{11} gives b11≤(λ1′−λ1)≤λ1′b_{11}\leq(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})\leq\lambda_{1}^{\prime}, which contradicts [[λ1′,λ2′,λ3′]]∈R[[\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}]]\in R.

If exactly two coefficients on the right-hand side of (16) are positive, without loss of generality, suppose that (λ1′−λ1)(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1}) and (λ2′−λ2)(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2}) are the two. Moving (λ3′−λ3)(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3}) to the other side gives

(λ′−λ)​d0+(λ3−λ3′)​d3=(λ1′−λ1)​d1+(λ2′−λ2)​d2.(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda)d_{0}+(\lambda_{3}-\lambda_{3}^{\prime})d_{3}=(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2})d_{2}. (18)

The above identity satisfies the conditions of the current theorem, thus the region {x>(λ1′−λ1),y>(λ2′−λ2)}\{x>(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1}),y>(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2})\} was deleted. Again, this contradicts [[λ1′,λ2′,λ3′]]∈R[[\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}]]\in R, since λ1′≥(λ1′−λ1)\lambda^{\prime}_{1}\geq(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1}) and λ2′≥(λ2′−λ2)\lambda^{\prime}_{2}\geq(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2}).

Now, the only case left is where all the coefficients in (16) are positive. We substitute μ=(λ′−λ)>0\mu=(\lambda^{\prime}-\lambda)>0 and μi=(λi′−λi)>0\mu_{i}=(\lambda_{i}^{\prime}-\lambda_{i})>0 for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. We have

μ​d0=μ1​d1+μ2​d2+μ3​d3\mu d_{0}=\mu_{1}d_{1}+\mu_{2}d_{2}+\mu_{3}d_{3} (19)

and since [[μ1,μ2,μ3]]≤[[λ1′,λ2′,λ3′]]∈R[[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]]\leq[[\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}]]\in R, we have [[μ1,μ2,μ3]]∈R[[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]]\in R. From the minimality of a00a_{00}, we get a00≤μa_{00}\leq\mu. Subtracting a00​d0=a01​d1+a02​d2+a03​d3a_{00}d_{0}=a_{01}d_{1}+a_{02}d_{2}+a_{03}d_{3} from (19) gives

(μ−a00)​d0=(μ1−a01)​d1+(μ2−a02)​d2+(μ3−a03)​d3.(\mu-a_{00})d_{0}=(\mu_{1}-a_{01})d_{1}+(\mu_{2}-a_{02})d_{2}+(\mu_{3}-a_{03})d_{3}. (20)

If μ=a00\mu=a_{00}, then (0,μ1,μ2,μ3)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}), hence the region associated to (μ1,μ2,μ3)(\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}) had been deleted, which contradicts [[μ1,μ2,μ3]]∈R[[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]]\in R.

Hence (μ−a00)>0(\mu-a_{00})>0. Now, we repeat the same case by case consideration with (20) as we did with (16), which results in all the coefficients in (20) being positive. However, this implies that the cube [[μ1,μ2,μ3]][[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]] is in the region associated to (a01,a02,a03)(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03}), which contradicts [[μ1,μ2,μ3]]∈R[[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]]\in R. ∎

Throughout this paper, RR denotes the collection of all cubes from the initial collection of cubes that are labeled with an element of the Apéry set. We will refer to equations of the forms (11), (12), (13) (where λi∈ℤ>0\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}) as the (2,2)(2,2)-type relations. In addition, we will refer to points that are constructed from the (2,2)(2,2)-type relations (as in Theorem 2.4) as the (2,2)(2,2)-type points.

2.3 LL-shapes

Define an LL-shape to be a subset of the initial collection of cubes such that:

  • •

    all its labels are elements of the Apéry set,

  • •

    every element of the Apéry set labels exactly one cube in it,

  • •

    if a cube [[a,b,c]][[a,b,c]], (a,b,c)∈ℕ3(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{N}^{3}, is not in it, then neither is any cube in the region associated to (a,b,c)(a,b,c).

This notion is adopted from [1] and is established in the literature.

Lemma 2.5.

Delete from RR one of the regions {x>a11}\{x>a_{11}\}, {y>a22}\{y>a_{22}\}, or {z>a33}\{z>a_{33}\}. Then every element of the Apéry set still labels some remaining cube.

Proof.

Delete the region {x>a11}\{x>a_{11}\} from RR (the other two cases follow analogously). If a11=b11a_{11}=b_{11}, there is nothing to prove; thus, suppose a11<b11a_{11}<b_{11}. Suppose to the contrary, that there is some element of the Apéry set that does not label any cube in R∩{x≤a11}R\cap\{x\leq a_{11}\}. By Theorem 2.4, then there exists [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈R[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in R with λ1≥a11\lambda_{1}\geq a_{11} that is labeled with the element in question. There exists a positive integer λ\lambda such that a11>(λ1−λ​a11)≥0a_{11}>(\lambda_{1}-\lambda a_{11})\geq 0. Using a11​d1=a12​d2+a13​d3a_{11}d_{1}=a_{12}d_{2}+a_{13}d_{3}, where a12,a13∈ℕa_{12},a_{13}\in\mathbb{N} (recall a11<b11a_{11}<b_{11}), we obtain

λ1​d1+λ2​d2+λ3​d3=(λ1−λ​a11)​d1+(λ2+λ​a12)​d2+(λ3+λ​a13)​d3.\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}d_{3}=(\lambda_{1}-\lambda a_{11})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}+\lambda a_{12})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}+\lambda a_{13})d_{3}. (21)

The cube [[λ1−λ​a11,λ2+λ​a12,λ3+λ​a13]][[\lambda_{1}-\lambda a_{11},\lambda_{2}+\lambda a_{12},\lambda_{3}+\lambda a_{13}]] has the same label as [[λ1,λ2,λ3]][[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]], hence it is in RR by Theorem 2.4. Since a11>(λ1−λ​a11)a_{11}>(\lambda_{1}-\lambda a_{11}), it is in R∩{x≤a11}R\cap\{x\leq a_{11}\} — contradiction. ∎

Lemma 2.6.

Delete from RR the regions {x>a11}\{x>a_{11}\}, {y>a22}\{y>a_{22}\}, and {z>a33}\{z>a_{33}\}. Then, in the resulting collection, each element of the Apéry set labels at most one cube.

Proof.

Suppose to the contrary, that for two distinct [[λ1,λ2,λ3]],[[λ1′,λ2′,λ3′]]∈R∩{x≤a11,y≤a22,z≤a33}[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]],[[\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}]]\in R\cap\{x\leq a_{11},y\leq a_{22},z\leq a_{33}\}, we have

λ1​d1+λ2​d2+λ3​d3=λ1′​d1+λ2′​d2+λ3′​d3\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}d_{3}=\lambda_{1}^{\prime}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}^{\prime}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}^{\prime}d_{3}
⟹(λ1′−λ1)​d1+(λ2′−λ2)​d2+(λ3′−λ3)​d3=0.\implies(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3})d_{3}=0.

If all coefficients above are zero, we have nothing to prove. Therefore either one or two coefficients above are positive. Regardless, without loss of generality, we can suppose that

(λ1′−λ1)​d1=(λ2−λ2′)​d2+(λ3−λ3′)​d3(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}=(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}-\lambda_{3}^{\prime})d_{3} (22)

where every coefficient above is nonnegative. However, (λ1′−λ1)(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1}) is positive, because otherwise all coefficients are zero. This implies a11≤(λ1′−λ1)≤λ1′a_{11}\leq(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})\leq\lambda_{1}^{\prime}, which contradicts [[λ1′,λ2′,λ3′]]∈R∩{x≤a11,y≤a22,z≤a33}[[\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}]]\in R\cap\{x\leq a_{11},y\leq a_{22},z\leq a_{33}\}. ∎

Proposition 2.7.

If ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle is primary, then R∩{z≤a33}R\cap\{z\leq a_{33}\} is an LL-shape.

Proof.

If ai​i=bi​ia_{ii}=b_{ii} for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3, then R=R∩{x≤a11,y≤a22,z≤a33}R=R\cap\{x\leq a_{11},y\leq a_{22},z\leq a_{33}\}, hence Lemma 2.6 yields the claim. Otherwise, we have ai​i<bi​ia_{ii}<b_{ii} for exactly one i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\}. In such case, Lemmas 2.5 and 2.6 yield the claim. ∎

Proposition 2.8.

Suppose that for ⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle we have a11=b11a_{11}=b_{11} and a22​d2=a33​d3a_{22}d_{2}=a_{33}d_{3}. Then there is a bijection f:R∩{y≥a22}→R∩{z≥a33}f:R\cap\{y\geq a_{22}\}\to R\cap\{z\geq a_{33}\} sending [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]↦[[λ1,λ2−a22,λ3+a33]][[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\mapsto[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}-a_{22},\lambda_{3}+a_{33}]]. Moreover, R∩{y≤a22}R\cap\{y\leq a_{22}\} and R∩{z≤a33}R\cap\{z\leq a_{33}\} are LL-shapes.

Proof.

For [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈R∩{y≥a22}[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in R\cap\{y\geq a_{22}\}, the cube [[μ1,μ2−a22,μ3+a33]][[\mu_{1},\mu_{2}-a_{22},\mu_{3}+a_{33}]] is in RR by Theorem 2.4, because it has the same label as [[λ1,λ2,λ3]][[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]], so it is labeled with an element of the Apéry set. Thus, the function f:[[λ1,λ2,λ3]]↦[[λ1,λ2−a22,λ3+a33]]f:[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\mapsto[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}-a_{22},\lambda_{3}+a_{33}]] maps R∩{y≥a22}R\cap\{y\geq a_{22}\} to R∩{z≥a33}R\cap\{z\geq a_{33}\} and is also clearly injective. Similarly, we obtain the injection f−1:R∩{z≥a33}→R∩{y≥a22}f^{-1}:R\cap\{z\geq a_{33}\}\to R\cap\{y\geq a_{22}\} sending [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]↦[[λ1,λ2+a22,λ3−a33]][[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\mapsto[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2}+a_{22},\lambda_{3}-a_{33}]], which yields that ff is a bijection.

Let T=R∩{z≤a33}T=R\cap\{z\leq a_{33}\}. Since ff preserves labels, every element of the Apéry set labels a cube in TT. Thus, to prove that TT is an LL-shape we only have to prove that it has distinct labels.

Otherwise, we have

μ1​d1+μ2​d2+μ3​d3=ν1​d1+ν2​d2+ν3​d3\mu_{1}d_{1}+\mu_{2}d_{2}+\mu_{3}d_{3}=\nu_{1}d_{1}+\nu_{2}d_{2}+\nu_{3}d_{3} (23)

where [[μ1,μ2,μ3]][[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]] and [[ν1,ν2,ν3]][[\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\nu_{3}]] are two distinct cubes in TT. Without loss of generality, suppose μ2≥ν2\mu_{2}\geq\nu_{2}.

If μ1≤ν1\mu_{1}\leq\nu_{1} and μ3≤ν3\mu_{3}\leq\nu_{3}, then

(μ2−ν2)​d2=(ν1−μ1)​d1+(ν3−μ3)​d3(\mu_{2}-\nu_{2})d_{2}=(\nu_{1}-\mu_{1})d_{1}+(\nu_{3}-\mu_{3})d_{3} (24)

where all coefficients above are nonnegative, which implies (μ2−ν2)≥a22(\mu_{2}-\nu_{2})\geq a_{22} (as [[μ1,μ2,μ3]]≠[[ν1,ν2,ν3]][[\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}]]\neq[[\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\nu_{3}]]). If ν3≥(ν3−μ3)≥a33\nu_{3}\geq(\nu_{3}-\mu_{3})\geq a_{33}, we get a contradiction with [[ν1,ν2,ν3]]∈T[[\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\nu_{3}]]\in T, hence (ν3−μ3)<a33(\nu_{3}-\mu_{3})<a_{33}. This gives

(μ2−ν2−a22)​d2+(a33−ν3+μ3)​d3=(ν1−μ1)​d1(\mu_{2}-\nu_{2}-a_{22})d_{2}+(a_{33}-\nu_{3}+\mu_{3})d_{3}=(\nu_{1}-\mu_{1})d_{1} (25)

where all coefficients above are nonnegative and (a33−ν3+μ3)(a_{33}-\nu_{3}+\mu_{3}) is positive. Hence (ν1−μ1)(\nu_{1}-\mu_{1}) is also positive, which implies ν1≥(ν1−μ1)≥a11=b11\nu_{1}\geq(\nu_{1}-\mu_{1})\geq a_{11}=b_{11}, contradicting [[ν1,ν2,ν3]]∈T[[\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\nu_{3}]]\in T.

If μ1>ν1\mu_{1}>\nu_{1} and μ3≤ν3\mu_{3}\leq\nu_{3}, then

(μ2−ν2)​d2+(μ1−ν1)​d1=(ν3−μ3)​d3(\mu_{2}-\nu_{2})d_{2}+(\mu_{1}-\nu_{1})d_{1}=(\nu_{3}-\mu_{3})d_{3} (26)

where all coefficients above are nonnegative and (μ1−ν1)(\mu_{1}-\nu_{1}) is positive, which implies ν3≥(ν3−μ3)≥a33\nu_{3}\geq(\nu_{3}-\mu_{3})\geq a_{33}, contradicting [[ν1,ν2,ν3]]∈T[[\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\nu_{3}]]\in T.

Lastly, if μ1≤ν1\mu_{1}\leq\nu_{1} and μ3>ν3\mu_{3}>\nu_{3}, then

(μ2−ν2)​d2+(μ3−ν3)​d3=(ν1−μ1)​d1(\mu_{2}-\nu_{2})d_{2}+(\mu_{3}-\nu_{3})d_{3}=(\nu_{1}-\mu_{1})d_{1} (27)

where all coefficients above are nonnegative and (μ3−ν3)(\mu_{3}-\nu_{3}) is positive, which implies ν1≥(ν1−μ1)≥a11=b11\nu_{1}\geq(\nu_{1}-\mu_{1})\geq a_{11}=b_{11}, so again a contradiction with [[ν1,ν2,ν3]]∈T[[\nu_{1},\nu_{2},\nu_{3}]]\in T.

Analogously, we obtain that R∩{y≤a22}R\cap\{y\leq a_{22}\} is an LL-shape. ∎

In particular, since secondary semigroups satisfy a11=b11a_{11}=b_{11} and a22​d2=a33​d3a_{22}d_{2}=a_{33}d_{3} by definition, Proposition 2.8 applies to all secondary semigroups.

Example 2.9.

3 Minimal presentations

In this section, we investigate the set of Betti elements for primary and secondary semigroups. We start with preliminary definitions and then proceed to the main results. Theorems 3.4 and 3.11 relate Betti elements to an LL-shape for primary and secondary semigroups respectively. Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7 determine the sets of factorizations of Betti elements arising from (2,2)(2,2)-type points in the primary case, while Lemmas 3.12 and 3.13 establish the analogous results for secondary semigroups. Finally, Lemma 3.8 characterizes the (2,2)(2,2)-type points which do not correspond to Betti elements in the primary case, while Lemmas 3.14 and 3.15 do the same in the secondary case. This framework will be used in Section 4 to study minimal presentations from a geometric perspective.

Bresinsky’s work [6], which underlies the bound in Theorem 1.2, contains results closely related to those of this section (cf. [6, Theorem 3]). Our approach differs in two main respects. First, in the classification of numerical semigroups with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, we distinguish primary and secondary semigroups, whereas Bresinsky introduced three families. Second, we relate Betti elements and minimal presentations to the Apéry set via an LL-shape, allowing us to make use of its geometric structure, whereas Bresinsky’s approach was commutative algebra centered.

Let SS be minimally generated by {d0,d1,…,dk}\{d_{0},d_{1},\dots,d_{k}\}. Two elements zz and z′z^{\prime} of ℕk+1\mathbb{N}^{k+1} are said to be ℛ\mathcal{R}-related if there exists a finite sequence z=z1,…,zp=z′z=z_{1},\dots,z_{p}=z^{\prime} in ℕk+1\mathbb{N}^{k+1} such that supp​(zi)∩supp​(zi+1)\text{supp}(z_{i})\cap\text{supp}(z_{i+1}) is nonempty for all i∈{1,…,p−1}i\in\{1,\dots,p-1\}. We write z​ℛ​z′z\,\mathcal{R}\,z^{\prime} in this case. We refer to the equivalence classes of φ−1​(s)\varphi^{-1}(s) under the relation ℛ\mathcal{R} as the ℛ\mathcal{R}-classes. An element s∈Ss\in S is called a Betti element if there exist two elements of φ−1​(s)\varphi^{-1}(s) that are not ℛ\mathcal{R}-related (i.e. φ−1​(s)\varphi^{-1}(s) has at least two ℛ\mathcal{R}-classes). The set of all Betti elements of SS is denoted Betti​(S)\text{Betti}(S).

Let ℛ1,…,ℛl\mathcal{R}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{R}_{l} be all the ℛ\mathcal{R}-classes of φ−1​(b)\varphi^{-1}(b) for some b∈Betti​(S)b\in\text{Betti}(S). [15] The set ρ=⋃b∈Betti​(S)ρb\rho=\bigcup_{b\in\text{Betti}(S)}\rho_{b} is a minimal presentation of SS and every minimal presentation of SS is of this form.

Lemma 3.5.

Suppose that SS is primary. If (−λ1,λ2,λ3)∈V(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in V satisfies

Note that λ2<a22\lambda_{2}<a_{22} and λ3<a33\lambda_{3}<a_{33} by the definition of VV.

Suppose μ0>0\mu_{0}>0. If μ2>0\mu_{2}>0, then by Lemma 2.3, no element of the Apéry set is a label in the region associated to (−μ1,λ2−μ2,λ3−μ3)(-\mu_{1},\lambda_{2}-\mu_{2},\lambda_{3}-\mu_{3}). This contradicts the fact [[0,λ2−1,λ3]]∈T[[0,\lambda_{2}-1,\lambda_{3}]]\in T, which holds since (−λ1,λ2,λ3)∈V(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in V. If μ3>0\mu_{3}>0, we get an analogous contradiction, hence μ2=μ3=0\mu_{2}=\mu_{3}=0.

Thus, suppose μ0=0\mu_{0}=0. If μ2≥λ2\mu_{2}\geq\lambda_{2}, then

(λ3−μ3)​d3=μ1​d1+(μ2−λ2)​d2(\lambda_{3}-\mu_{3})d_{3}=\mu_{1}d_{1}+(\mu_{2}-\lambda_{2})d_{2} (44)

Hence (λ3−μ3)=0(\lambda_{3}-\mu_{3})=0, which gives (μ0,μ1,μ2,μ3)=(0,0,λ2,λ3)(\mu_{0},\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3})=(0,0,\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}). Since λ0>0\lambda_{0}>0, by Lemma 2.3, no cube labeled with an element of the Apéry set is in the region associated to (μ1−λ1,μ2,μ3)(\mu_{1}-\lambda_{1},\mu_{2},\mu_{3}). This contradicts the fact [[0,λ2−1,λ3−1]]∈T[[0,\lambda_{2}-1,\lambda_{3}-1]]\in T, which holds since (−λ1,λ2,λ3)∈V(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in V.

The same argument applies to (λ1,−λ2,λ3)(\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}) and (λ1,λ2,−λ3)∈V(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3})\in V. ∎

which results in only one ℛ\mathcal{R}-class.

which gives a contradiction, since a00>(μ0−λ0−λ​a00)>0a_{00}>(\mu_{0}-\lambda_{0}-\lambda a_{00})>0.

Lemma 3.8.

Suppose that SS is primary. If (−λ1,λ2,λ3)∈V(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in V satisfies

λ0​d0+λ1​d1=λ2​d2+λ3​d3∉Betti​(S)\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{1}d_{1}=\lambda_{2}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}d_{3}\notin\textup{Betti}(S)

with λi∈ℤ>0\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}, then λ0=a00\lambda_{0}=a_{00} and λ1<a11\lambda_{1}<a_{11}. An analogous statement holds for (λ1,−λ2,λ3)(\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}) and (λ1,λ2,−λ3)∈V(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3})\in V.

Proof.

The condition λ0​d0+λ1​d1∉Betti​(S)\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{1}d_{1}\notin\textup{Betti}(S) implies a00​d0≠a11​d1a_{00}d_{0}\neq a_{11}d_{1}, and λ0≥a00\lambda_{0}\geq a_{00} or λ1≥a11\lambda_{1}\geq a_{11}, by Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7. Also, note that λ2<a22\lambda_{2}<a_{22} and λ3<a33\lambda_{3}<a_{33} by the definition of VV.

Suppose λ1≥a11\lambda_{1}\geq a_{11}. For (a10,0,a12,a13)∈φ−1​(a11​d1)(a_{10},0,a_{12},a_{13})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{11}d_{1}), we have

where (λ1−a11)≥0(\lambda_{1}-a_{11})\geq 0. If (λ2−a12)<0(\lambda_{2}-a_{12})<0, then λ3≥(λ3−a13)≥a33\lambda_{3}\geq(\lambda_{3}-a_{13})\geq a_{33}, which is a contradiction. If (λ3−a13)<0(\lambda_{3}-a_{13})<0, we get the same contradiction. Hence (λ2−a12),(λ3−a13)≥0(\lambda_{2}-a_{12}),(\lambda_{3}-a_{13})\geq 0. If max⁡{a12,a13}>0\max\{a_{12},a_{13}\}>0, then by Lemma 2.3, no cube labeled with an element of the Apéry set is in the region associated to (−λ1+a11,λ2−a12,λ3−a13)(-\lambda_{1}+a_{11},\lambda_{2}-a_{12},\lambda_{3}-a_{13}). This contradicts the fact [[0,λ2−1,λ3−1]]∈T[[0,\lambda_{2}-1,\lambda_{3}-1]]\in T, which holds since (−λ1,λ2,λ3)∈V(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in V. Hence a12=a13=0a_{12}=a_{13}=0 and a11​d1=a10​d0a_{11}d_{1}=a_{10}d_{0}. This gives a10>a00a_{10}>a_{00}, as a00​d0≠a11​d1a_{00}d_{0}\neq a_{11}d_{1}. For (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}), we have

a11​d1=(a10−a00)​d0+a01​d1+a02​d2+a03​d3a_{11}d_{1}=(a_{10}-a_{00})d_{0}+a_{01}d_{1}+a_{02}d_{2}+a_{03}d_{3} (51)

which gives a01=0a_{01}=0, as otherwise we would get a contradiction with the minimality of a11a_{11}. Therefore, we have max⁡{a02,a03}>0\max\{a_{02},a_{03}\}>0 and

(λ0+a10−a00)​d0+(λ1−a11+a01)​d1=(λ2−a02)​d2+(λ3−a03)​d3.(\lambda_{0}+a_{10}-a_{00})d_{0}+(\lambda_{1}-a_{11}+a_{01})d_{1}=(\lambda_{2}-a_{02})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}-a_{03})d_{3}. (52)

Since (λ0+a10−a00)>0(\lambda_{0}+a_{10}-a_{00})>0, no cube labeled with an element of the Apéry set is in the region associated to (−λ1+a11−a01,λ2−a02,λ3−a03)(-\lambda_{1}+a_{11}-a_{01},\lambda_{2}-a_{02},\lambda_{3}-a_{03}), by Lemma 2.3. Again, this contradicts the fact [[0,λ2−1,λ3−1]]∈T[[0,\lambda_{2}-1,\lambda_{3}-1]]\in T. Therefore λ1<a11\lambda_{1}<a_{11}.

If λ0>a00\lambda_{0}>a_{00}, then for (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}), we have

3.2 Secondary case

Lemma 3.9.

Suppose that SS satisfies a11=b11a_{11}=b_{11} and a22​d2=a33​d3a_{22}d_{2}=a_{33}d_{3}. If b∈Betti​(S)b\in\textup{Betti}(S) labels a cube in RR, then b=a22​d2=a33​d3b=a_{22}d_{2}=a_{33}d_{3}.

Proof.

Consider a factorization (0,λ1,λ2,λ3)∈φ−1​(b)(0,\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in\varphi^{-1}(b) with [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈R[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in R. Let (λ0′,λ1′,λ2′,λ3′)(\lambda_{0}^{\prime},\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}) be a distinct factorization of bb. We have

(λ1−λ1′)​d1+(λ2−λ2′)​d2+(λ3−λ3′)​d3=λ0′​d0.(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{\prime})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}-\lambda_{3}^{\prime})d_{3}=\lambda_{0}^{\prime}d_{0}. (54)
  • •

    If all coefficients on the left-hand side of (54) are nonnegative, then λ0′>0\lambda_{0}^{\prime}>0, as the two factorizations are distinct. This contradicts [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈R[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in R by Lemma 2.3.

  • •

    Suppose that exactly one coefficient on the left-hand side of (54) is nonnegative. If (λ1−λ1′)(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{\prime}) is the nonnegative coefficient, then λ1≥(λ1−λ1′)≥a11=b11\lambda_{1}\geq(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{\prime})\geq a_{11}=b_{11}, which contradicts [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈R[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in R. Therefore, without loss of generality, suppose that (λ2−λ2′)(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime}) is the nonnegative coefficient. This gives

    (λ2−λ2′)​d2=λ0′​d0+(λ1′−λ1)​d1+(λ3′−λ3)​d3(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})d_{2}=\lambda_{0}^{\prime}d_{0}+(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}+(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3})d_{3} (55)

    where every coefficient above is nonnegative, which implies (λ2−λ2′)≥a22(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})\geq a_{22} (since (λ2−λ2′)≠0(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})\neq 0, as (λ3′−λ3)>0(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3})>0). If λ0′>0\lambda_{0}^{\prime}>0, then λ2≥(λ2−λ2′)≥b22\lambda_{2}\geq(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})\geq b_{22}, which contradicts [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈R[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in R, hence λ0′=0\lambda_{0}^{\prime}=0. There exists λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} such that a22>λ2−λ2′−λ​a22≥0a_{22}>\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda a_{22}\geq 0. Using a22​d2=a33​d3a_{22}d_{2}=a_{33}d_{3}, we obtain

Lemma 3.14.

Suppose that SS is secondary. No element (λ1,−λ2,λ3)∈V(\lambda_{1},-\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\in V satisfies

with λi∈ℤ>0\lambda_{i}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0}.

Proof.

(λ0−a00)​d0+λ2​d2+(a11−λ1)​d1=λ3​d3(\lambda_{0}-a_{00})d_{0}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}+(a_{11}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}=\lambda_{3}d_{3} (80)

where all above coefficients are nonnegative. Since (a11−λ1)>0(a_{11}-\lambda_{1})>0, we get λ3≥a33\lambda_{3}\geq a_{33}, which is a contradiction.

where all above coefficients are nonnegative. Since (a33−λ3)>0(a_{33}-\lambda_{3})>0, we get λ1≥a11\lambda_{1}\geq a_{11}, which is a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 3.15.

Suppose that SS is secondary. If (λ1,λ2,−λ3)∈V(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3})\in V satisfies

λ0​d0+λ3​d3=λ1​d1+λ2​d2∉Betti​(S)\lambda_{0}d_{0}+\lambda_{3}d_{3}=\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}\notin\textup{Betti}(S)

4 t⁡(S)t(S) and η⁡(S)\eta(S)

This section is devoted to proving Theorem 1.4. We begin with a series of lemmas relating the type to the set VV, culminating in Theorem 4.10. We then turn to results linking VV to η⁡(S)\eta(S), concluding with Corollary 4.17, from which Theorem 1.4 follows.

Let S=⟨d0,d1,d2,d3⟩S=\langle d_{0},d_{1},d_{2},d_{3}\rangle be a numerical semigroup with embedding dimension four that is ordered. Let TT, RR, VV, and UU be as in the previous sections.

4.1 t⁡(S)t(S) and VV

A finite and nonempty subset FF of the initial collection of cubes is called a cube figure if for every (a,b,c)∈ℕ3(a,b,c)\in\mathbb{N}^{3} with [[a,b,c]]∉F[[a,b,c]]\notin F, no cube in the region associated to (a,b,c)(a,b,c) is in FF. For a cube figure FF, a cube [[a,b,c]]∈F[[a,b,c]]\in F is called a corner of FF if [[a+1,b,c]],[[a,b+1,c]],[[a,b,c+1]]∉F[[a+1,b,c]],[[a,b+1,c]],[[a,b,c+1]]\notin F.

Recall from (4) that

PF(S)={s−d0∣s∈Ap(S,d0),s+di∉Ap(S,d0) for i=1,2,3}.PF(S)=\{s-d_{0}\mid s\in\textup{Ap}(S,d_{0}),s+d_{i}\notin\textup{Ap}(S,d_{0})\text{ for }i=1,2,3\}. (84)

Thus, since RR is the collection of all cubes labeled with an element of the Apéry set, P​F​(S)PF(S) is the set of all labels of corners of RR, and t⁡(S)t(S) is the number of such distinct labels.

Lemma 4.1.

There exists at most one (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) that satisfies (a01,a02,a03)∈V∖{(b11,0,0),(0,b22,0),(0,0,b33)}(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in V\setminus\{(b_{11},0,0),(0,b_{22},0),(0,0,b_{33})\}.

If SS is secondary, then φ−1​(a00​d0)={(a00,0,0,0),(0,a11,0,0)}\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0})=\{(a_{00},0,0,0),(0,a_{11},0,0)\} (and by definition a11=b11a_{11}=b_{11}), so no such (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) exists in this case.

If (a01,a02,a03)=(0,0,a33)(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})=(0,0,a_{33}), then a33=b33a_{33}=b_{33} (as a00>0a_{00}>0), which contradicts (a01,a02,a03)≠(0,0,b33)(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\neq(0,0,b_{33}). If (a01,a02,a03)∈{(a11,0,0),(0,a22,0)}(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\{(a_{11},0,0),(0,a_{22},0)\}, we get an analogous contradiction, therefore a0​i,a0​i′<ai​ia_{0i},a_{0i}^{\prime}<a_{ii}. We have

(a01−a01′)​d1+(a02−a02′)​d2+(a03−a03′)​d3=0.(a_{01}-a_{01}^{\prime})d_{1}+(a_{02}-a_{02}^{\prime})d_{2}+(a_{03}-a_{03}^{\prime})d_{3}=0. (85)

This implies a01≥(a01−a01′)≥a11a_{01}\geq(a_{01}-a_{01}^{\prime})\geq a_{11}, which is a contradiction. ∎

Lemma 4.3.

Every integer that labels a corner of RR also labels a corner of TT.

Proof.

Consider a corner [[a,b,c]][[a,b,c]] of RR that is in the region R∩{z≥a33}R\cap\{z\geq a_{33}\} (that is c≥a33c\geq a_{33}). There exists λ∈ℕ\lambda\in\mathbb{N} such that a33>c−λ​a33≥0a_{33}>c-\lambda a_{33}\geq 0, for which we have C=[[a+λa31,b+λa32,c−λa33]]∈R∩{z≤a33}=TC=[[a+\lambda a_{31},b+\lambda a_{32},c-\lambda a_{33}]]\in R\cap\{z\leq a_{33}\}=T, since CC has the same label as [[a,b,c]][[a,b,c]]. We claim that CC is a corner of TT. If not, then there exists [[a′,b′,c′]]∈T[[a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}]]\in T with C<[[a′,b′,c′]]C<[[a^{\prime},b^{\prime},c^{\prime}]]. However, this implies [[a,b,c]]<[[a′−λ​a31,b′−λ​a32,c′+λ​a33]]∈R[[a,b,c]]<[[a^{\prime}-\lambda a_{31},b^{\prime}-\lambda a_{32},c^{\prime}+\lambda a_{33}]]\in R, which contradicts the fact that [[a,b,c]][[a,b,c]] is a corner of RR. ∎

Let t′t^{\prime} denote the number of corners of TT and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be the set of the corners of TT that are not corners of RR. Since TT is an LL-shape, the corners of TT have distinct labels. This fact, combined with Lemma 4.3, yields t′=|𝒯|+t⁡(S)t^{\prime}=|\mathcal{T}|+t(S).

For the semigroups ⟨196,225,256,289⟩\langle 196,225,256,289\rangle and ⟨145,203,74,111⟩\langle 145,203,74,111\rangle from Example 2.9, shown in Figures 6 and 6, respectively, the cubes shown in blue are all the corners of TT that are also corners of RR, and the cubes shown in magenta are all the cubes in 𝒯\mathcal{T}.

Lemma 4.4.

If SS is primary, then 2​t​(S)≥t′≥t⁡(S)2t(S)\geq t^{\prime}\geq t(S).

Proof.

If a33=b33a_{33}=b_{33}, then t′=t⁡(S)t^{\prime}=t(S), so suppose that a33<b33a_{33}<b_{33}. Consider any [[λ1,λ2,λ3]]∈𝒯[[\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}]]\in\mathcal{T}. Suppose that there exists (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) with (a01,a02,a03)∈V(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in V and a01​a02​a03>0a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}>0. By Lemmas 4.1 and 4.2 we know that this point is unique. Let T′T^{\prime} be the figure obtained by removing from the initial collection of cubes all the regions associated to each of V∖{(a01,a02,a03)}V\setminus\{(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\}. Note that the sets of stair cubes of TT and T′T^{\prime} are equal. Moreover, T′T^{\prime} satisfies the assumptions of Proposition 4.8, hence it has at most two odd corners.

Now, deleting from T′T^{\prime} the region associated to (a01,a02,a03)(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03}) will yield TT. We claim that this operation can add at most six new odd corners. Note that any new odd corner could not have been a corner of T′T^{\prime} — by the definition, a corner that is not odd in T′T^{\prime} cannot become an odd corner merely because cubes were deleted. Thus every new odd corner must touch the region associated to (a01,a02,a03)(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03}) with one of its faces.

Assume, for contradiction, that seven new odd corners appear. This means that three of them touch the same side of the region associated to (a01,a02,a03)(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03}). Without loss of generality, suppose that [[x1,y1,a03−1]],[[x2,y2,a03−1]],[[x3,y3,a03−1]][[x_{1},y_{1},a_{03}-1]],[[x_{2},y_{2},a_{03}-1]],[[x_{3},y_{3},a_{03}-1]] are three distinct odd corners, where x1>x2>x3≥a01x_{1}>x_{2}>x_{3}\geq a_{01} and y3>y2>y1≥a02y_{3}>y_{2}>y_{1}\geq a_{02}. We have [[x2+1,y2,0]]∈T[[x_{2}+1,y_{2},0]]\in T or [[x2,y2+1,0]]∈T[[x_{2},y_{2}+1,0]]\in T. If [[x2+1,y2,0]]∈T[[x_{2}+1,y_{2},0]]\in T, then there exists x1≥λ>x2x_{1}\geq\lambda>x_{2}, y2≥μ>y1y_{2}\geq\mu>y_{1}, and a03−1≥ν>0a_{03}-1\geq\nu>0, such that [[λ,μ,ν]]∉F[[\lambda,\mu,\nu]]\notin F and [[λ−1,μ,ν]],[[λ,μ−1,ν]],[[λ,μ,ν−1]]∈F[[\lambda-1,\mu,\nu]],[[\lambda,\mu-1,\nu]],[[\lambda,\mu,\nu-1]]\in F. This implies (λ,μ,ν)∈V(\lambda,\mu,\nu)\in V, which by Lemma 4.2, contradicts Lemma 4.1. On Figure 14, we can see an example of such a situation, where P=(λ,μ,ν)P=(\lambda,\mu,\nu). If [[x2,y2+1,0]]∈T[[x_{2},y_{2}+1,0]]\in T, we proceed analogously.

Thus, since T′T^{\prime} has at most two odd corners, TT can have at most eight odd corners. Each non-odd corner [[a,b,c]][[a,b,c]] of TT has at least one associated stair cube, chosen from [[0,b,c]],[[a,0,c]],[[a,b,0]][[0,b,c]],[[a,0,c]],[[a,b,0]]. Every stair cube is associated to at most one corner of TT, hence |𝒮|≥t′−8|\mathcal{S}|\geq t^{\prime}-8. ∎

Theorem 4.10.

If SS is primary, then 4​t​(S)+1≥|V∗|≥t⁡(S)−114t(S)+1\geq|V^{*}|\geq t(S)-11. If SS is secondary, then 2​t​(S)+3≥|V∗|≥t⁡(S)−52t(S)+3\geq|V^{*}|\geq t(S)-5.

Suppose that there exists (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) such that (a01,a02,a03)∈V(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in V and a01​a02​a03>0a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}>0. Then, by Lemma 4.1, the point (a01,a02,a03)∈V(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in V is unique and there does not exist (0,a01′,a02′,a03′)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01}^{\prime},a_{02}^{\prime},a_{03}^{\prime})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) such that (a01′,a02′,a03′)∈V(a_{01}^{\prime},a_{02}^{\prime},a_{03}^{\prime})\in V and exactly one among a01′,a02′,a03′a_{01}^{\prime},a_{02}^{\prime},a_{03}^{\prime} is zero. |V∗|≥|𝒮|−3≥t′−11≥t⁡(S)−11|V^{*}|\geq|\mathcal{S}|-3\geq t^{\prime}-11\geq t(S)-11 (89)

which are the result of Lemmas 4.6, 4.9, and 4.4, respectively.

Suppose that there does not exist (0,a01,a02,a03)∈φ−1​(a00​d0)(0,a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0}) such that (a01,a02,a03)∈V(a_{01},a_{02},a_{03})\in V and a01​a02​a03>0a_{01}a_{02}a_{03}>0. Then, we have the following chain of inequalities:

|V∗|≥|𝒮|−4≥t′−6≥t⁡(S)−6|V^{*}|\geq|\mathcal{S}|-4\geq t^{\prime}-6\geq t(S)-6 (90)

which are the result of Lemmas 4.6, 4.9, and 4.4, respectively. As t⁡(S)−6≥t⁡(S)−11t(S)-6\geq t(S)-11, the first claim follows.

Suppose that SS is secondary. The upper bound for |V∗||V^{*}| is due to the following chain of inequalities:

which are the result of Lemmas 4.6, 4.7, and 4.5, respectively. Hence, we have the following chain of inequalities:

|V∗|≥|𝒮|−3≥t′−5≥t⁡(S)−5|V^{*}|\geq|\mathcal{S}|-3\geq t^{\prime}-5\geq t(S)-5 (92)

Lemma 4.11.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, let (−λ1,λ2,λ3)(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3}) and (−λ1′,λ2′,λ3′)(-\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}) be distinct points in 𝒩\mathcal{N} (where λi>0\lambda_{i}>0). a00​d0+λ1​d1\displaystyle a_{00}d_{0}+\lambda_{1}d_{1} =λ2​d2+λ3​d3,\displaystyle=\lambda_{2}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}d_{3}, (93)
a00​d0+λ1′​d1\displaystyle a_{00}d_{0}+\lambda_{1}^{\prime}d_{1} =λ2′​d2+λ3′​d3,\displaystyle=\lambda_{2}^{\prime}d_{2}+\lambda_{3}^{\prime}d_{3}, (94)

where λi,λi′<ai​i\lambda_{i},\lambda_{i}^{\prime}<a_{ii} for i=1,2,3i=1,2,3. Subtracting (93) from (94) gives

(λ1−λ1′)​d1+(λ2′−λ2)​d2+(λ3′−λ3)​d3=0.(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{\prime})d_{1}+(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2})d_{2}+(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3})d_{3}=0. (95)

Since (−λ1,λ2,λ3)≠(−λ1′,λ2′,λ3′)(-\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},\lambda_{3})\neq(-\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}), not all coefficients above are zero. Without loss of generality, suppose (λ1−λ1′)>0(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{\prime})>0, (λ2′−λ2)≤0(\lambda_{2}^{\prime}-\lambda_{2})\leq 0, (λ3′−λ3)≤0(\lambda_{3}^{\prime}-\lambda_{3})\leq 0. This implies λ1≥(λ1−λ1′)≥a11\lambda_{1}\geq(\lambda_{1}-\lambda_{1}^{\prime})\geq a_{11}, which is a contradiction. ∎

Proof.

a00​d0+λ3​d3\displaystyle a_{00}d_{0}+\lambda_{3}d_{3} =λ1​d1+λ2​d2,\displaystyle=\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}, (96)
a00​d0+λ3′​d3\displaystyle a_{00}d_{0}+\lambda_{3}^{\prime}d_{3} =λ1′​d1+λ2′​d2,\displaystyle=\lambda_{1}^{\prime}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}^{\prime}d_{2}, (97)

where λ3,λ3′<a33\lambda_{3},\lambda_{3}^{\prime}<a_{33} Since T=R∩{z≤a33}T=R\cap\{z\leq a_{33}\}, we have λ1,λ1′<b11=a11\lambda_{1},\lambda_{1}^{\prime}<b_{11}=a_{11}.

(λ3−λ3′)​d3+(λ1′−λ1)​d1=(λ2−λ2′)​d2(\lambda_{3}-\lambda_{3}^{\prime})d_{3}+(\lambda_{1}^{\prime}-\lambda_{1})d_{1}=(\lambda_{2}-\lambda_{2}^{\prime})d_{2} (98)

where all above coefficients are nonnegative, as otherwise we would get a contradiction with λ3<a33\lambda_{3}<a_{33} or λ1<a11\lambda_{1}<a_{11}. where all above coefficients are positive. This contradicts φ−1​(a00​d0)={(a00,0,0,0),(0,a11,0,0)}\varphi^{-1}(a_{00}d_{0})=\{(a_{00},0,0,0),(0,a_{11},0,0)\}. ∎

Let

Suppose that there exist distinct (λ1,λ2,−λ3)(\lambda_{1},\lambda_{2},-\lambda_{3}) and (λ1′,λ2′,−λ3′)∈V∗∖𝒩(\lambda_{1}^{\prime},\lambda_{2}^{\prime},-\lambda_{3}^{\prime})\in V^{*}\setminus\mathcal{N} (where λi>0\lambda_{i}>0) such that λ1​d1+λ2​d2=λ1′​d1+λ2′​d2\lambda_{1}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}d_{2}=\lambda_{1}^{\prime}d_{1}+\lambda_{2}^{\prime}d_{2}. Let ρ\rho be a minimal presentation of SS and let ρ∗={(a,b)∈ℕ4×ℕ4∣(a,b)∈ρ,|supp(a)|=|supp(b)|=2}\rho^{*}=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb{N}^{4}\times\mathbb{N}^{4}\mid(a,b)\in\rho,|\textup{supp}(a)|=|\textup{supp}(b)|=2\}. To proceed, we require a result of Bresinsky [6].

Lemma 4.14.

[6, Corollary 2] There exists a minimal presentation ρ\rho such that η⁡(S)−|ρ∗|≤4\eta(S)-|\rho^{*}|\leq 4.

Lemma 4.15.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1, and Theorems 2.4 and 3.4, we have

Betti​(S)=U0⊔{a00​d0,a11​d1,a22​d2,a33​d3}.\textup{Betti}(S)=U_{0}\sqcup\{a_{00}d_{0},a_{11}d_{1},a_{22}d_{2},a_{33}d_{3}\}. (102)

Lemma 2.1 tells us that (a00,0,0,0)(a_{00},0,0,0) is the only element in its ℛ\mathcal{R}-class. The same is true for (0,a11,0,0)(0,a_{11},0,0), (0,0,a22,0)(0,0,a_{22},0), and (0,0,0,a33)(0,0,0,a_{33}), so the sets on the right-hand side of (102) are indeed disjoint.

If there exists a factorization in ⋃i=03φ−1​(ai​i​di)\bigcup_{i=0}^{3}\varphi^{-1}(a_{ii}d_{i}) that is distinct from the four canonical ones, then a00​d0,a11​d1,a22​d2,a33​d3a_{00}d_{0},a_{11}d_{1},a_{22}d_{2},a_{33}d_{3} together contribute at least three elements to ρ\rho by Lemma 2.1 and Theorem 3.1. From Lemmas 3.6 and 3.7 we know that every element of U0U_{0} has exactly two ℛ\mathcal{R}-classes, so each contributes exactly one element to ρ\rho, by Theorem 3.1. This, combined with the previous paragraph, gives η⁡(S)≥|U0|+3\eta(S)\geq|U_{0}|+3.

Suppose, for contradiction, that η⁡(S)−|U0|>4\eta(S)-|U_{0}|>4. By Lemma 2.1, there do not exist z1,z2∈φ−1​(ai​i​di)z_{1},z_{2}\in\varphi^{-1}(a_{ii}d_{i}) such that |supp​(z1)|=|supp​(z2)|=2|\textup{supp}(z_{1})|=|\textup{supp}(z_{2})|=2 and supp​(z1)∩supp​(z2)=∅\textup{supp}(z_{1})\cap\textup{supp}(z_{2})=\varnothing. Thus in every minimal presentation ρ\rho, there will be more than 44 elements that are not in ρ∗\rho^{*}. This gives a contradiction with Lemma 4.14, therefore η⁡(S)≤|U0|+4\eta(S)\leq|U_{0}|+4. ∎

Lemma 4.16.

If SS is secondary, then |U0|+6≥η⁡(S)≥|U0|+2|U_{0}|+6\geq\eta(S)\geq|U_{0}|+2.

Proof.

By Lemma 2.1 and Theorems 2.4 and 3.11, we have

U0⊔{a00​d0,a22​d2}⊆Betti​(S)⊆U0∪{a00​d0,a22​d2,b22​d2,b33​d3}.U_{0}\sqcup\{a_{00}d_{0},a_{22}d_{2}\}\subseteq\textup{Betti}(S)\subseteq U_{0}\cup\{a_{00}d_{0},a_{22}d_{2},b_{22}d_{2},b_{33}d_{3}\}. (103)

However, if b23>b33b_{23}>b_{33}, then (b30CLOSE(b_{30}, b31b_{31}, b32b_{32}, OPEN(b23−b33))∈φ−1​(b22​d2)(b_{23}-b_{33}))\in\varphi^{-1}(b_{22}d_{2}), which is a contradiction, since b30,(b23−b33)>0b_{30},(b_{23}-b_{33})>0. Hence b23=b33b_{23}=b_{33} and b22​d2=b33​d3b_{22}d_{2}=b_{33}d_{3}. Therefore, in the current case, b22​d2b_{22}d_{2} and b33​d3b_{33}d_{3} together contribute at most three elements to ρ\rho, by Theorem 3.1, since b22​d2=b33​d3b_{22}d_{2}=b_{33}d_{3} has at most four ℛ\mathcal{R}-classes.

Therefore, by (103), we have η⁡(S)≤|U0|+2+4=|U0|+6\eta(S)\leq|U_{0}|+2+4=|U_{0}|+6. ∎

Corollary 4.17.

If SS is primary, then 4​t​(S)+5≥η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)−114t(S)+5\geq\eta(S)\geq t(S)-11. If SS is secondary, then 2​t​(S)+9≥η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)−42t(S)+9\geq\eta(S)\geq t(S)-4.

Proof.

Suppose that SS is primary. The lower bound for η⁡(S)\eta(S) follows from the chain of inequalities:

η⁡(S)≥|U0|+3=|V∗∖𝒩|+3≥|V∗|≥t⁡(S)−11\eta(S)\geq|U_{0}|+3=|V^{*}\setminus\mathcal{N}|+3\geq|V^{*}|\geq t(S)-11 (104)

which are the result of Lemmas 4.15, 4.13, 4.11, and Theorem 4.10, respectively. Moreover, the upper bound for η⁡(S)\eta(S) is due to the following chain of inequalities:

η⁡(S)≤|U0|+4=|V∗∖𝒩|+4≤|V∗|+4≤4​t​(S)+5\eta(S)\leq|U_{0}|+4=|V^{*}\setminus\mathcal{N}|+4\leq|V^{*}|+4\leq 4t(S)+5 (105)

which are the result of Lemmas 4.15, 4.13, and Theorem 4.10, respectively.

Suppose that SS is secondary. The lower bound for η⁡(S)\eta(S) is due to the following chain of inequalities:

η⁡(S)≥|U0|+2=|V∗∖𝒩|+2≥|V∗|+1≥t⁡(S)−4\eta(S)\geq|U_{0}|+2=|V^{*}\setminus\mathcal{N}|+2\geq|V^{*}|+1\geq t(S)-4 (106)

which are the result of Lemmas 4.16, 4.13, 4.12, and Theorem 4.10, respectively. Moreover, the upper bound for η⁡(S)\eta(S) is due to the following chain of inequalities:

η⁡(S)≤|U0|+6=|V∗∖𝒩|+6≤|V∗|+6≤2​t​(S)+9\eta(S)\leq|U_{0}|+6=|V^{*}\setminus\mathcal{N}|+6\leq|V^{*}|+6\leq 2t(S)+9 (107)

which are the result of Lemmas 4.16, 4.13, and Theorem 4.10, respectively. ∎

For t⁡(S)≥2t(S)\geq 2, the inequality 4​t​(S)+5≥2​t​(S)+94t(S)+5\geq 2t(S)+9 holds, so Corollary 4.17 implies Theorem 1.4 in this case. Recall that t⁡(S)=1t(S)=1 is equivalent to SS being symmetric [11]. This allows us to use the following result to resolve the case t⁡(S)=1t(S)=1.

Theorem 4.18.

[5] If SS is symmetric with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, then η⁡(S)∈{3,5}\eta(S)\in\{3,5\}.

Since 5≤9=4⋅1+55\leq 9=4\cdot 1+5, this completes the proof of Theorem 1.4.

5 Closing remarks

The bounds of Theorem 1.4 can most likely be improved. To improve the bound η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)−11\eta(S)\geq t(S)-11, we propose the following conjecture.

Conjecture 5.1.

If SS is a numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, then η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)+1\eta(S)\geq t(S)+1.

We expect that η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)+1\eta(S)\geq t(S)+1 is the best possible bound, since no numerical semigroup with e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4 and η⁡(S)≤t⁡(S)\eta(S)\leq t(S) is currently known. In contrast, the situation where η⁡(S)=t⁡(S)+1\eta(S)=t(S)+1 is quite common among numerical semigroups with embedding dimension four. For example, S=⟨77,85,89,131⟩S=\langle 77,85,89,131\rangle has e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, t⁡(S)=3t(S)=3, and η⁡(S)=4\eta(S)=4. Likewise, S=⟨76,99,143,223⟩S=\langle 76,99,143,223\rangle has e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, t⁡(S)=6t(S)=6, η⁡(S)=7\eta(S)=7, and S=⟨195,200,209,226⟩S=\langle 195,200,209,226\rangle has e⁡(S)=4e(S)=4, t⁡(S)=8t(S)=8, η⁡(S)=9\eta(S)=9. The equation η⁡(S)=t⁡(S)+1\eta(S)=t(S)+1 is also satisfied for all numerical semigroups with e⁡(S)=3e(S)=3 (Theorem 1.1).

Remark 5.2.

In higher embedding dimension, the inequality η⁡(S)≥t⁡(S)+1\eta(S)\geq t(S)+1 is false in general, already for embedding dimension five. For example, S=⟨86,133,143,155,198⟩S=\langle 86,133,143,155,198\rangle has e⁡(S)=5e(S)=5 and t⁡(S)=η⁡(S)=10t(S)=\eta(S)=10. Likewise, S=⟨161,177,196,207,225⟩S=\langle 161,177,196,207,225\rangle has e⁡(S)=5e(S)=5, t⁡(S)=18t(S)=18, η⁡(S)=16\eta(S)=16, and (a more extreme example) S=⟨6072,6307,7965,8702,9423⟩S=\langle 6072,6307,7965,8702,9423\rangle has e⁡(S)=5e(S)=5, t⁡(S)=53t(S)=53, η⁡(S)=40\eta(S)=40.

Remark 5.3.

The results of Section 2, together with the results of Section 3 concerning primary semigroups, appeared earlier in the preprint [7].
